## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes standardized procedures for measuring tree diameter
at breast height (DBH), conducting fixed-area plot-based forest
inventories, and estimating basal area using prism or angle-gauge
sampling. These measurements are fundamental to characterizing forest
structure, estimating stand density and biomass, monitoring tree growth,
and providing inputs to allometric equations for carbon accounting
[@avery2002; @westfall2020]. The measurement conventions follow the
USDA Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) national
standards [@usfs_fia2023].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** All EA Program field sites with tree cover, including
  riparian forests, oak woodlands, mixed conifer stands, and planted
  trees at restoration and campus sites
- **Does not apply to:** Shrubs with DBH below 2.5 cm (use
  [SOP-F603](SOP-F603-vegetation-transect-surveys.qmd) for shrub cover);
  timber cruising for commercial harvest; urban tree risk assessment
- **Location:** All EA Program terrestrial field sites with woody
  vegetation


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve plot design and minimum DBH threshold           |
| Trained Personnel | Measure trees and record data per this SOP              |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent measurement        |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Dead or leaning trees (snags, widow-makers) may shed
  branches. Look up before working under any tree. Do not measure trees
  during high winds.
- **Biological:** Poison oak, ticks, stinging insects, and snakes in
  wooded habitats. Wasp nests may be present in tree cavities.
- **Terrain:** Steep slopes in forested areas increase fall risk. Use
  caution when navigating uneven terrain with equipment.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Long pants
- [ ] Hard hat (in areas with overhead hazard trees)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Tick repellent

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd). Work in
pairs in remote forested areas.


## 5. Equipment and Materials

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Diameter tape (DBH tape, metric)      | Graduated in diameter units (pi tape); reads directly in cm |
| Standard measuring tape (50 m)        | For establishing plot boundaries         |
| Clinometer (Suunto or equivalent)     | For measuring tree height (optional)     |
| Basal area factor (BAF) prism or angle gauge | For variable-radius plot sampling   |
| GPS unit or smartphone                | Per [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd) |
| Field notebook or data sheet          | Pre-printed inventory form (Appendix A)  |
| Compass                               | For plot layout and stem mapping         |
| Flagging tape                         | For marking plot center and measured trees |
| Tree tags and nails (aluminum)        | For permanent plot re-measurement        |
| Paint marker or timber crayon         | For marking the DBH measurement point    |
| Laser rangefinder (optional)          | For measuring tree height and distances  |
| Calculator                            | For basal area and density calculations  |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Measuring DBH

DBH is measured at 1.37 m (4.5 ft) above ground level on the uphill
side of the tree [@avery2002; @usfs_fia2023].

1. Identify the measurement height: 1.37 m above the ground surface on
   the uphill side of the tree. If the ground is level, measure from
   any side.
2. Wrap the diameter tape around the trunk at 1.37 m, perpendicular to
   the axis of the trunk (not perpendicular to the slope).
3. Ensure the tape is snug against the bark, not twisted, and level.
   Read the diameter directly from the DBH tape to the nearest 0.1 cm.
4. Record the measurement in the field notebook or data sheet.

**Special cases:**

| Situation                         | Measurement Rule                     |
|:----------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|
| Tree on a slope                   | Measure at 1.37 m from the uphill side of the base |
| Forked below 1.37 m               | Measure each fork as a separate tree |
| Forked at or above 1.37 m         | Measure as one tree below the fork   |
| Swelling or abnormality at 1.37 m | Measure above and below the abnormality and average |
| Leaning tree                      | Measure 1.37 m along the underside of the trunk |
| Buttressed tree                   | Measure above the buttress where the trunk becomes cylindrical |

::: {.callout-tip}
### Tip
For permanent monitoring plots, mark the DBH measurement point on the
bark with a paint marker or timber crayon so that subsequent
measurements are taken at the exact same height. For long-term
studies, tag each tree with a numbered aluminum tag nailed above
breast height.
:::

### 6.2 Fixed-Area Plot Inventory

Fixed-area plots are the standard method for forest inventory
[@vanLaar2007]. Plot size depends on tree density.

| Tree Density      | Recommended Plot Size     | Radius (circular) |
|:------------------|:--------------------------|:-------------------|
| Dense forest      | 0.01 ha (100 m^2^)       | 5.64 m             |
| Moderate forest   | 0.04 ha (400 m^2^)       | 11.28 m            |
| Open woodland     | 0.10 ha (1000 m^2^)      | 17.84 m            |

**Procedure:**

1. Navigate to the plot center and record GPS coordinates per
   [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd).
2. Mark the plot center with a stake or flagging tape.
3. For circular plots, use the measuring tape as a radius to determine
   which trees are inside the plot boundary. A tree is "in" if more
   than half of its trunk at DBH lies within the plot radius.
4. Measure and record the following for every tree with DBH at or above
   the minimum threshold (typically 2.5 cm or 10 cm, as specified by
   the project):
   - Species (common name and/or scientific name)
   - DBH (cm)
   - Condition class: live, standing dead (snag), leaning
   - Crown class (optional): dominant, co-dominant, intermediate,
     suppressed
   - Height (optional; measured with a clinometer or rangefinder)
5. Record the total number of stems and species per plot.

### 6.3 Variable-Radius Plot Sampling (Basal Area Prism)

The BAF prism provides a rapid estimate of stand basal area without
establishing fixed plot boundaries [@avery2002; @grosenbaugh1952].

1. Stand at the sample point and hold the BAF prism at arm's length,
   looking through it at each surrounding tree at breast height.
2. For each tree, the prism refracts the image of the trunk. Compare
   the offset image to the original:
   - **Tree is "in":** The offset image overlaps the unrefracted trunk.
     Count the tree.
   - **Tree is "out":** The offset image is completely separated from
     the unrefracted trunk. Do not count.
   - **Borderline:** The offset image just touches the trunk edge.
     Count every other borderline tree.
3. Rotate 360 degrees, counting all "in" trees.
4. Calculate basal area:

$$
\text{Basal area (m}^2\text{/ha)} = n \times \text{BAF}
$$

where $n$ is the number of "in" trees and BAF is the basal area factor
of the prism (typically 1, 2, 4, or 5 m^2^/ha per tree counted;
check the prism label).

### 6.4 Tree Height Measurement (Optional)

Use a clinometer or laser rangefinder to measure total tree height
[@vanLaar2007]:

1. Stand at a known horizontal distance from the tree base (e.g.,
   15--30 m; measure with a tape or rangefinder).
2. Sight the tree top through the clinometer and record the angle to
   the top ($\alpha$).
3. Sight the tree base and record the angle to the base ($\beta$).
   If the base is below eye level, $\beta$ is negative.
4. Calculate height:

$$
H = D \times (\tan\alpha - \tan\beta)
$$

where $D$ is the horizontal distance (m) and $H$ is the total height
(m).


## 7. Derived Calculations

### 7.1 Basal Area per Tree

$$
\text{BA (m}^2\text{)} = \frac{\pi}{4} \times \left(\frac{\text{DBH}}{100}\right)^2
$$

where DBH is in cm.

### 7.2 Stand Density and Basal Area per Hectare

$$
\text{Trees/ha} = \frac{n}{\text{plot area (ha)}}
$$

$$
\text{BA/ha (m}^2\text{/ha)} = \frac{\sum \text{BA}_i}{\text{plot area (ha)}}
$$

### 7.3 Biomass Estimation

Above-ground biomass can be estimated using published allometric
equations of the form:

$$
\text{Biomass (kg)} = a \times \text{DBH}^b
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are species-specific coefficients from published
sources [@chojnacky2014; @jenkins2003]. Document the allometric
equation, source, and species used in the project README.

Large-diameter trees store a disproportionately large fraction of
aboveground carbon in most forest types; accurate measurement of the
largest individuals in a stand is therefore critical for unbiased
biomass and carbon stock estimates [@lutz2018].


## 8. Quality Control

- Measure DBH twice (wrap the tape, read, remove, re-wrap, re-read).
  The two readings should agree within 0.5 cm. Record the mean.
- On 10% of plots, have a second observer independently measure all
  trees. DBH measurements should agree within 1 cm; tree counts should
  match exactly.
- Verify the diameter tape calibration at the start of each field
  season by measuring a cylinder of known diameter.
- For permanent plots, verify that tags are intact and measurement
  points are correctly located at each re-measurement.

## 11. Training Record

Before conducting tree measurements independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate correct DBH measurement technique, including special
   cases (forks, slopes, buttresses)
3. Participate in a supervised plot inventory
4. Demonstrate BAF prism technique with results within 10% of the
   trainer's count
5. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
